summary:
Gliluv Maritime Holdings, LLC (client, Buyer) bought all of the stock of Saltreach Marine Services, Inc., a tanker and bulk-carrier ship management company, from Dreisend Shipping Group, Ltd. (Seller). The Stock Purchase Agreement is governed by New York law. It was signed December 1, 2025 and closed January 15, 2026, for $64,000,000, with $6,400,000 placed in escrow. At closing the parties also signed a Transition Services Agreement under which Seller provides crew management, vessel-performance data, and ERP and chartering-system services to Buyer, and an Escrow Agreement with Pelham Trust Company, N.A. A post-closing written consent of Buyer's board, dated March 20, 2026, records that Seller delivered its Closing Statement on February 9, 2026. In that consent the board resolves to dispute a $1,900,000 working-capital overstatement. The folder also contains the Target's office lease, which is in order.

The review should surface five problems:
- The adjustment objection window lapsed before the board acted.
- An uncapped TSA indemnity runs from Buyer to Seller.
- The Escrow Agreement, which controls under the SPA's precedence clause, strips the environmental carve-out from the cap.
- The tax representations and the pre-closing tax indemnity survive only six months.
- Seller is left free to assign the SPA and TSA, including to a competitor.

issues.label: expired notice window
issues.description:
Two provisions read together show that Buyer's right to dispute the post-closing adjustment has already lapsed.

- SPA Section 2.4(b) gives Buyer 30 days after receipt of Seller's Closing Statement to deliver a written objection. If Buyer does not object in time, the Closing Statement becomes final and binding.
- Buyer's Board Written Consent (D3), dated March 20, 2026, recites in Recital B that Seller delivered the Closing Statement on February 9, 2026. The objection window therefore closed on March 11, 2026.
- In the same consent the board resolves to dispute a $1,900,000 working-capital overstatement and authorizes management to deliver the objection. That shows Buyer has not accepted the statement.

The objection was not authorized until nine days after the window closed. Under SPA Section 2.4(b) the Closing Statement is now final and binding. Unless Seller agrees otherwise, Buyer has lost its $1.9M adjustment claim.
detect_terms: within thirty (30) days after receipt of the Closing Statement
issues.expected_finding: Measured from the February 9, 2026 delivery date recited in the March 20, 2026 board consent, Buyer's 30-day objection window under SPA Section 2.4(b) expired March 11, 2026, so the Closing Statement is binding and the $1.9M overstatement is lost unless Buyer promptly delivers the objection and obtains Seller's written waiver or extension of the deadline.

issues.label: uncapped indemnity
issues.description:
Under TSA Section 8.3, Buyer as Recipient indemnifies Seller as Provider for all Losses arising from the Services or from Recipient's use of them. This includes Losses caused by Provider's own negligence, with an exception only for gross negligence or willful misconduct. Section 8.3 states that this indemnity is not subject to Section 8.4 or any other limitation.

By contrast, Section 8.4 caps Provider's own liability at the fees paid under the TSA. The SPA's cap in Section 9.5 does not help Buyer, because it reaches only Article IX claims. SPA Section 11.8 also makes the TSA control as to the Services.

The result is that Buyer bears unlimited exposure for crew-management and vessel-operations services that are run by Seller.
detect_terms: shall not be subject to Section 8.4 or any other limitation
issues.expected_finding: TSA Section 8.3 exposes Buyer to unlimited indemnity liability to Seller, including for Seller's own negligence, while Seller's liability is capped at TSA fees under Section 8.4, so Buyer should seek to make the indemnity mutual, exclude Provider negligence, and subject it to a cap.

issues.label: liability cap carve-out conflict
issues.description:
The Escrow Agreement removes a carve-out from the Seller's cap that the SPA was meant to preserve.

- SPA Section 9.5(b) excludes the Environmental Indemnity under Section 9.2(c) from the Seller cap. That indemnity covers pre-closing oil pollution, MARPOL and ballast-water liabilities. The cap is equal to the $6,400,000 Escrow Amount.
- Escrow Agreement Section 5.3 makes the Escrow Fund the sole and exclusive source of recovery for all indemnification claims under Article IX of the SPA, expressly including claims under Section 9.2(c).
- SPA Section 11.8 provides that the Escrow Agreement governs escrow recovery. That precedence clause lets Section 5.3 control rather than curing it.

Taken together, these provisions limit Buyer's recovery for potentially large OPA 90 and pollution liabilities to the $6.4M escrow.
detect_terms: sole and exclusive source of recovery
issues.expected_finding: Because SPA Section 11.8 lets the Escrow Agreement govern escrow recovery, Escrow Agreement Section 5.3 effectively caps the Section 9.2(c) Environmental Indemnity at the $6.4M Escrow Fund despite SPA Section 9.5(b), and Buyer should amend Section 5.3 (and Section 11.8) to preserve direct recourse against Seller for the excluded claims.

issues.label: indemnity survival gap
issues.description:
Three SPA provisions combine to cut off tax claims early.

- Section 9.1 provides that the Tax Representations in Section 4.11 survive only until six months after the Closing Date. With a January 15, 2026 closing, that is July 15, 2026.
- The Pre-Closing Tax indemnity in Section 9.2(d) is made subject to the survival period in Section 9.1.
- Section 9.4 bars any claim not noticed before the applicable survival period expires.

Tax exposures typically surface only on audit within the three-year limitations period. Examples are U.S. gross transportation tax and tonnage-tax assessments on the fleet. New York law enforces contractually shortened survival periods. Buyer would therefore lose these claims well before audits conclude, even though the escrow remains in place until July 2027.
detect_terms: six (6) months after the Closing Date
issues.expected_finding: Under SPA Sections 9.1, 9.2(d) and 9.4, the tax representations and Pre-Closing Tax indemnity expire six months after the January 15, 2026 Closing Date (July 15, 2026), long before tax audits would reveal liabilities, so survival should be extended to at least 60 days after the applicable statute of limitations.

issues.label: unrestricted assignment
issues.description:
The assignment provisions restrict only Buyer.

- TSA Section 12.4 provides that assignment of the TSA is governed by SPA Section 11.5, mutatis mutandis.
- SPA Section 11.5 says that Buyer may not assign without Seller's consent. It says nothing about Seller.

Under New York law, contract rights and obligations are freely assignable unless the contract restricts assignment. Seller can therefore assign or delegate:
- the TSA, including access to the Company's crew, chartering and vessel-performance data, to a competing ship manager; and
- its SPA indemnity obligations, to an entity with fewer assets.

Buyer has no consent right in either case.
detect_terms: Section 11.5 of the Purchase Agreement, mutatis mutandis
Buyer may not assign this Agreement
issues.expected_finding: Because TSA Section 12.4 imports SPA Section 11.5, which restricts only Buyer, Seller may freely assign the TSA and SPA (including to a competitor that would gain access to the Company's operational data or to a thinly capitalized assignee of its indemnity obligations), so both should be amended to require Buyer's consent to any Seller assignment or delegation.
